//: Debezium PostgreSQL source connector. Property names are Debezium 3.x.
Four properties commonly copied from older tutorials fail silently or loudly
against 3.x, so they are called out here:
plugin.name                   defaults to decoderbufs, which needs a server
extension that is not installed; pgoutput is
built into Postgres 10+ and is set explicitly
PG_REPL_PASSWORD is substituted by scripts/bootstrap.sh at registration time,
so this file stays committable with no credential in it.
Registered with PUT /connectors/<name>/config, never POST. PUT is
create-or-update, so re-running bootstrap is idempotent; POST returns 409 on
the second call and breaks any retry.
plugin.name: pgoutput
slot.name: ${PG_REPL_SLOT}
publication.name: ${PG_PUBLICATION}
//table_include_list: wb.cdc_heartbeat is captured deliberately, alongside the three business
tables. It is what makes connector liveness measurable downstream:
the heartbeat row is updated on a timer, so lag measured against it reflects
whether the CONNECTOR is keeping up. Lag measured against a business table
instead conflates a stalled connector with a table that simply has not changed,
and an idle dimension would then raise a CDC alert every night.
//time_and_number_encoding: time.precision.mode=connect makes DATE arrive as int32 days since epoch and
TIMESTAMP as int64 millis, both Kafka Connect logical types, instead of
Debezium's adaptive microsecond variants. TIMESTAMPTZ is a ZonedTimestamp
ISO-8601 string either way. Pinning the mode means the ClickHouse casts are
written against one documented encoding rather than whichever default the
decimal.handling.mode=double is belt and braces: the source columns are
already double precision precisely so no NUMERIC is base64-encoded on the
wire, but if a NUMERIC is ever added this keeps it a JSON number.
//heartbeat: The single most important operational setting here. A logical replication
slot only advances its confirmed_flush_lsn when the consumer acknowledges an
event. If the captured tables are idle while other activity on the cluster
keeps producing WAL, the slot stays pinned and WAL accumulates behind it
until the disk fills, with nothing in the connector looking wrong.
The heartbeat writes to a captured table on a timer, which produces an event
the connector acknowledges, which drags the slot forward. It is a keepalive
for the replication slot, and max_slot_wal_keep_size on the server is the
backstop if it is ever missing.
heartbeat.action.query: UPDATE wb.cdc_heartbeat SET beat_at = now(), beat_count = beat_count + 1 WHERE id = 1
//slot_lifecycle: slot.drop.on.stop=false so a restart resumes from the recorded LSN instead of
re-snapshotting. The consequence is that stopping the stack leaves a slot
retaining WAL, which is why `make down` drops it explicitly and the README
//transform: ExtractNewRecordState flattens Debezium's before/after envelope to the new row
state, which is what a warehouse landing table wants.
delete.tombstone.handling.mode=rewrite is what makes deletes visible: instead
of dropping the delete or emitting a null-valued tombstone, it emits the row
with a __deleted marker. Without it, a delete either vanishes (and the
warehouse keeps a row the source no longer has) or arrives as a null the
add.fields carries the operation and the log coordinates through, and __lsn is
what the ReplacingMergeTree uses as its version column.
//tombstones: false because the rewrite mode above already represents deletes as real rows.
Leaving it true would additionally emit a null-valued record per delete, which
the ClickHouse Kafka engine would have to parse and discard.
